entries.meaning: To look at something before it is finished or made public. ---
examples: You can preview the first chapter for free.
The teacher previewed the test questions with the class.
I'm previewing the slides before I print them.

entries.meaning: To work out what something badly written or unclear says. ---
examples: I can't decipher my own handwriting.
She finally deciphered the doctor's note.
We spent an hour deciphering a letter from 1890.
entries.contrast: Spelled with ph: decipher, never decypher.

entries.meaning: To work out the meaning of something written in code or in an unfamiliar form. ---
examples: Children learn to decode words before they read fluently.
He decoded the message in under an hour.
She is decoding her grandmother's shorthand.

entries.meaning: To move text or images up or down on a screen. ---
examples: Scroll down to the comments.
He scrolled through the article looking for the quote.
She was scrolling on her phone all evening.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scroll the page), intransitive (scroll down)

entries.meaning: To press a button on a mouse or a spot on a screen to choose something. ---
examples: Click the blue link at the bottom of the page.
I clicked on the ad by mistake.
Stop clicking — the page is still loading.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (click the link), intransitive (click on the icon)
entries.contrast: You click on a link or simply click it; both are normal American usage.

entries.meaning: To load the newest version of a page or a list. ---
examples: Refresh the page and the table will load.
I refreshed my inbox every five minutes.
The app is refreshing the headlines automatically.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (refresh the page), intransitive (the feed refreshes every minute)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after sh: refreshes.

entries.meaning: To save a page so that you can find it again easily. ---
examples: Bookmark this recipe before you close the tab.
I bookmarked the article to read on the train.
He has bookmarked half the dictionary.

entries.meaning: To mark part of a text with bright color, or to draw attention to it. ---
examples: Highlight every word you don't know.
She highlighted three paragraphs in yellow.
The review kept highlighting the book's weak ending.

entries.meaning: To draw a line under a word or a sentence. ---
examples: Underline the verb in each sentence.
He underlined his name twice.
The editor is underlining the same mistake again.

entries.meaning: To add notes to a text to explain it or comment on it. ---
examples: Students annotate the poem line by line.
She annotated the margins in pencil.
This copy has been annotated by three different readers.

entries.meaning: To repeat someone's words wrongly. ---
examples: Headlines often misquote scientists.
The paper misquoted her twice in one story.
He says he was misquoted about the budget.

entries.meaning: To name a book, article, or person as the source of your information. ---
examples: You must cite every source you use.
The paper cited a study from 2019.
He has cited the same website four times.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like site (a place) and sight (vision).

entries.meaning: To mention a source or an earlier text in your own writing. ---
examples: Reference the original study in a footnote.
The article referenced three other papers.
She kept referencing a movie I had never seen.

entries.meaning: To put someone else's idea into your own words. ---
examples: Paraphrase the paragraph in one sentence.
He paraphrased the law for us in plain English.
I'm paraphrasing, but that was her point.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (paraphrase a passage), intransitive (I'm paraphrasing)

entries.meaning: To copy someone else's writing and present it as your own. ---
examples: Never plagiarize, even by accident.
He plagiarized half his essay from a blog.
She was caught plagiarizing in her first semester.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (plagiarize a paper), intransitive (students who plagiarize)
entries.contrast: American plagiarize; British plagiarise.

entries.meaning: To go over the main points of something again briefly. ---
examples: Let me recap what we agreed on.
The host recapped last week's episode.
She is recapping the chapter for anyone who missed it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (recap the chapter), intransitive (let me recap)
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: recapped, recapping.

entries.meaning: To say or write something again, usually more clearly. ---
examples: Restate the question in your own words.
He restated his argument in the conclusion.
She is restating the rules for the new students.

entries.meaning: To write out in full what someone said or what a recording contains. ---
examples: I have to transcribe the interview tonight.
She transcribed the tape word for word.
The app is transcribing the meeting as we speak.

entries.meaning: To say words aloud for someone or something to write down. ---
examples: Dictate the address and I'll type it.
The doctor dictated her notes after each visit.
He was dictating letters all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dictate a letter), intransitive (he dictates to his phone)

entries.meaning: To add a written translation of the speech at the bottom of a film or video. ---
examples: They subtitle every episode in four languages.
The movie was subtitled in English.
A small team is subtitling the documentary now.

entries.meaning: To replace the original speech in a film with speech in another language. ---
examples: German television dubs most American shows.
The film was dubbed into Italian.
The studio is dubbing the series for Latin America.
entries.contrast: Doubles the b: dubbed, dubbing.

entries.meaning: To give the different forms of a verb. ---
examples: Conjugate the verb to be in the past tense.
We conjugated irregular verbs all week.
He is still conjugating them out loud in the hallway.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (conjugate the verb), intransitive (this verb conjugates irregularly)

entries.meaning: To write a word with a capital letter at the beginning. ---
examples: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence.
She capitalized every noun, as if she were writing German.
Days and months are capitalized in English.
entries.contrast: American capitalize; British capitalise.

entries.meaning: To put commas, periods, and other marks into a piece of writing. ---
examples: Punctuate the dialogue correctly.
He punctuated the sentence with three exclamation points.
The letter was badly punctuated.

entries.meaning: To join two words with a hyphen, or to break a word at the end of a line. ---
examples: Do you hyphenate 'well known' before a noun?
The editor hyphenated every compound adjective.
Her last name is hyphenated.

entries.meaning: To make a word or a title shorter. ---
examples: You can abbreviate 'Street' as 'St.'
They abbreviated the title on the cover.
'Doctor' is usually abbreviated to 'Dr.'

entries.meaning: To print or type words in slanted letters. ---
examples: Italicize the titles of books.
She italicized all the foreign words.
The quotation is italicized on page two.

entries.meaning: To put words or names in the order of the alphabet. ---
examples: Alphabetize the list by last name.
He alphabetized his whole bookshelf one weekend.
The index is alphabetized, so it's easy to search.

entries.meaning: To start a line of writing further in from the margin. ---
examples: Indent the first line of every paragraph.
She indented the long quotation.
The paragraphs are not indented in this style.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (indent the first line), intransitive (indent before you start)

entries.meaning: To give each item in a list or a set its own number. ---
examples: Number your answers from one to ten.
He numbered the pages by hand.
The chapters are numbered in Roman numerals.

entries.meaning: To end with the same sound as another word. ---
examples: 'Cat' and 'hat' rhyme.
He rhymed 'silver' with nothing at all.
She is rhyming every other line.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rhyme 'moon' with 'June'), intransitive ('cat' and 'hat' rhyme)
entries.contrast: Silent h after the r: rhyme, like rhythm.

entries.meaning: To write something using a keyboard. ---
examples: Please type your name in the first box.
She typed the whole essay in one night.
He is still typing with two fingers.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (type a letter), intransitive (he types fast)

entries.meaning: To type something again, usually to correct it. ---
examples: You'll have to retype the last page.
I retyped the address twice and still got it wrong.
She is retyping the letter with today's date.

entries.meaning: To put text or an image you have copied into another place. ---
examples: Copy the link and paste it in the chat.
I pasted the table into the report.
He was pasting the same paragraph into every email.

entries.meaning: To put something into a text in the right place. ---
examples: Insert a comma after the name.
The editor inserted two footnotes.
She is inserting the photos into the document.
entries.contrast: Verb in-SURT, noun IN-surt.

entries.meaning: To remove writing so that nothing is left. ---
examples: Erase the pencil marks before you hand it in.
He erased the wrong answer and wrote a new one.
The board had already been erased.

entries.meaning: To remove text or a file from a document or a computer. ---
examples: Delete the last paragraph — it repeats the first.
I deleted the email by mistake.
She has deleted every draft but one.

entries.meaning: To arrange how a text looks on the page or the screen. ---
examples: Format the list with bullet points.
He formatted the essay in twelve-point type.
The tables are formatted differently on every page.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: formatted, formatting.

entries.meaning: To give something a new name. ---
examples: Rename the file before you send it.
They renamed the magazine last year.
The folder has been renamed twice this week.

entries.meaning: To correct and improve a piece of writing before it is published. ---
examples: Could you edit my cover letter?
She edited the story down to 800 words.
He is editing the school magazine this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (edit an essay), intransitive (she edits for a living)
entries.contrast: One t: edited, editing — the stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double.

entries.meaning: To find the mistakes in something and make them right. ---
examples: Correct the spelling in red.
She corrected thirty papers last night.
The teacher is correcting our essays now.

entries.meaning: To read a text carefully for mistakes before it is printed or sent. ---
examples: Could you proof this before I send it?
He proofed the newsletter twice and still missed a typo.
She is proofing the last few pages.
entries.contrast: A short form of proofread, which is irregular: proofread, proofread.

entries.meaning: To change the wording of a document or a law slightly. ---
examples: We may amend the contract next week.
Congress amended the bill twice.
The rules have been amended since you read them.

entries.meaning: To say something again in different words so that it is clearer. ---
examples: Let me rephrase the question.
She rephrased the sentence three times.
He kept rephrasing the same idea.

entries.meaning: To change the wording of a written text without changing its meaning. ---
examples: Reword the ending so it sounds friendlier.
The lawyer reworded one whole clause.
They are rewording the instructions for beginners.

entries.meaning: To make a piece of writing shorter while keeping the main points. ---
examples: Condense the report to two pages.
She condensed the chapter into a single summary.
The article was condensed for the newsletter.

entries.meaning: To make something easier to read or to understand. ---
examples: Simplify the language for younger readers.
He simplified the instructions after the first complaint.
This text has been simplified for beginners.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: simplifies, simplified, but simplifying.

entries.meaning: To tell a story, or to speak the words that go with a film or recording. ---
examples: Who narrates the audiobook?
The author narrated her own memoir.
A child in the back row is narrating the whole movie.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (narrate a story), intransitive (he narrates beautifully)

entries.meaning: To record something in writing or on film so that there is proof of it. ---
examples: Document every payment you make.
She documented the whole trip in a blog.
The changes are documented in the appendix.
entries.contrast: The verb ends -ment (DAHK-yuh-ment); the noun ends in a schwa (DAHK-yuh-muhnt).

entries.meaning: To add pictures to a text, or to make a point clear with an example. ---
examples: Small drawings illustrate each chapter.
Her sister illustrated the children's book.
He is illustrating a cookbook this spring.

entries.meaning: To give a book, article, or piece of music a name. ---
examples: What should we title the article?
She titled the essay 'Small Hours'.
The album is titled after his daughter.

entries.meaning: To write something down quickly and briefly. ---
examples: Jot the number on the envelope.
He jotted a few lines in his notebook.
She was jotting notes all through the call.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: jotted, jotting.

entries.meaning: To write something quickly and messily. ---
examples: He scribbles notes on the back of receipts.
She scribbled her address on a napkin.
The baby was scribbling all over the book.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scribble a note), intransitive (scribble in the margin)

entries.meaning: To draw little pictures without thinking, usually while doing something else. ---
examples: He doodles through every meeting.
She doodled flowers in the margin.
I was doodling instead of taking notes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (doodle a face), intransitive (doodle in a notebook)

entries.meaning: To fill a drawing with color using crayons or pencils. ---
examples: Let the kids color the last page.
She colored the whole sky purple.
He is coloring inside the lines for once.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (color a picture), intransitive (the kids colored quietly)
entries.contrast: American color, colored, coloring; British colour, coloured, colouring.

entries.meaning: To say or write more about something you have already mentioned. ---
examples: Could you elaborate a little?
She elaborated on her answer in the second paragraph.
He is elaborating on a point nobody questioned.
entries.contrast: Takes on: elaborate on an idea. The verb ends -rayt; the adjective elaborate ends -ruht.

entries.meaning: To tell or write the story of something that happened. ---
examples: Recount the events in the order they happened.
He recounted the whole argument to his brother.
She is recounting her first year in Chicago.
entries.contrast: ri-KOWNT means 'tell the story'; REE-kownt means 'count again'.

entries.meaning: To describe or show a person or place in a particular way in a book or film. ---
examples: The novel portrays a small town in winter.
She portrayed her father as a hero.
Teachers are often portrayed as saints in these books.
entries.contrast: Vowel + -y: portrays, portrayed — the y does not change.

entries.meaning: To show or describe something in words or pictures. ---
examples: The article depicts life in a border town.
The painting depicted a harvest.
Poverty is rarely depicted honestly on television.

entries.meaning: To print a book or an article again. ---
examples: They will reprint the novel with a new cover.
The magazine reprinted her essay in June.
The book has been reprinted eleven times.

entries.meaning: To make a paper copy of a page with a machine. ---
examples: Photocopy your passport and keep it somewhere safe.
She photocopied the whole chapter for the class.
He is photocopying the forms now.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: photocopies, photocopied, like copy.

entries.meaning: To send a copy of a document over a phone line. ---
examples: The clinic asks you to fax the form.
She faxed the signed page this morning.
Doctors are still faxing prescriptions to pharmacies.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es: faxes.

entries.meaning: To make an exact copy of something. ---
examples: Duplicate the file before you edit it.
She duplicated the handout for the whole class.
The slides are being duplicated for everyone.
entries.contrast: The verb ends -kayt; the noun and adjective end -kuht (a duplicate copy).

entries.meaning: To publish a text again, often in a new form. ---
examples: They plan to republish her diaries next fall.
The essay was republished online a week later.
A university press is republishing his early novels.

entries.meaning: To pass something around so that many people see it. ---
examples: Circulate the draft before Friday.
Someone circulated the memo to the whole office.
Rumors were circulating long before the article appeared.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (circulate a draft), intransitive (rumors circulate)

entries.meaning: To cut out parts of a text, film, or letter that someone in authority finds unacceptable. ---
examples: Some governments censor the news.
The prison censored his letters.
Whole pages had been censored before the file was released.
entries.contrast: Censor (cut out) is not censure (criticize officially) or sensor (a device).

entries.meaning: To black out parts of a document before it is made public. ---
examples: They redact names to protect privacy.
The agency redacted half the report.
The emails were released in redacted form.

entries.meaning: To take back something you said or published because it was wrong. ---
examples: The paper had to retract the story.
He retracted the statement the next day.
Two of the study's claims have been retracted.

entries.meaning: To give a story, person, or work a prominent place in a publication or program. ---
examples: The magazine features a new poet every month.
They featured her essay on the front page.
The issue featuring the interview sold out.

entries.meaning: To offer an idea for a story, book, or project to someone who might buy it. ---
examples: Pitch the story to an editor first.
She pitched three articles and sold two.
He is pitching his novel to agents this month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pitch a story), intransitive (pitch to an editor)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after ch: pitches.

entries.meaning: To rewrite a book or story so that it can be a film, a play, or a version for other readers. ---
examples: They plan to adapt the novel for television.
She adapted the play for young audiences.
The book has been adapted three times already.
entries.contrast: Adapt (change something) is not adopt (take as your own).

entries.meaning: To judge a piece of work carefully and say what is good and bad about it. ---
examples: Classmates critique each other's drafts.
The professor critiqued my argument line by line.
They spent the hour critiquing the opening chapter.
entries.contrast: Pronounced kri-TEEK; a critic is KRIT-ik.

entries.meaning: To judge how good something is, often by giving it stars or points. ---
examples: Readers rate the book four stars out of five.
She rated the hotel poorly in her review.
The app is rated for ages twelve and up.

entries.meaning: To send a file from your own device to the internet or a server. ---
examples: Upload the essay before midnight.
He uploaded the wrong version by mistake.
She is uploading the photos now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (upload a file), intransitive (it's still uploading)

entries.meaning: To copy a file from the internet onto your own device. ---
examples: Download the form and print it.
I downloaded the book last night.
The article can be downloaded free.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (download a book), intransitive (the file is downloading)

entries.meaning: To store documents or messages for the long term instead of deleting them. ---
examples: Archive the old emails instead of deleting them.
The library archived every issue of the paper.
Her letters have been archived at the university.

entries.meaning: To put together a book, list, or report out of many separate pieces. ---
examples: They compile a new dictionary every decade.
She compiled his poems into one volume.
He is compiling a list of sources.

entries.meaning: To list things in order so that they can be found again. ---
examples: Volunteers catalog the donated books.
She cataloged the whole collection in a month.
The photographs are being cataloged by year.
entries.contrast: American catalog, cataloged; British catalogue, catalogued.

entries.meaning: To write down events, hours, or numbers in an official record. ---
examples: Drivers log every trip they make.
The nurse logged his temperature at noon.
She has been logging her reading all year.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: logged, logging.

entries.meaning: To mark something so that someone will notice it and deal with it. ---
examples: Flag any sentence you don't understand.
The editor flagged three factual errors.
Two emails are flagged as urgent.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: flagged, flagging.

entries.meaning: To attach a name or a keyword to a photo, post, or file. ---
examples: Don't tag me in that photo.
She tagged the post with three keywords.
He is tagging everyone who was there.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: tagged, tagging.

entries.meaning: To write a short line of text under a photograph or a picture. ---
examples: Caption each photo with a name and a date.
She captioned the picture 'First day of school'.
All the videos are captioned for deaf viewers.

entries.meaning: To send someone a written message online or on a phone. ---
examples: Message me when you land.
He messaged her three times before she answered.
She is messaging the whole group now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (message a friend), intransitive (we messaged all night)

entries.meaning: To write regularly on a personal website. ---
examples: She blogs about teaching English.
He blogged every single day for a year.
They have been blogging since college.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: blogged, blogging.

entries.meaning: To publish someone else's post again on your own page. ---
examples: Feel free to repost the announcement.
Hundreds of people reposted the article.
She is reposting it with a comment of her own.

entries.meaning: To write your name on a document to show that it is yours or that you agree. ---
examples: Sign at the bottom of the second page.
She signed the lease yesterday.
The letter came back because it wasn't signed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sign a letter), intransitive (sign at the bottom)
entries.contrast: Silent g: sign rhymes with fine, but signature is SIG-nuh-chur.

entries.meaning: To sign your name on something for someone who admires your work. ---
examples: Writers often autograph books after a reading.
He autographed my copy of the novel.
She is autographing posters in the lobby.

entries.meaning: To write a short personal message in a book or on an object. ---
examples: Authors sometimes inscribe books for their readers.
She inscribed the copy to her old teacher.
The ring is inscribed with a date.

entries.meaning: To write your initials on a document to show you have read or approved it. ---
examples: Initial each page of the contract.
She initialed the changes in the margin.
Every correction has been initialed by the manager.
entries.contrast: American initialed, initialing; British doubles the l: initialled.

entries.meaning: To write the day's date on a document. ---
examples: Sign and date the form at the bottom.
He dated the letter March 3.
The check was dated last year, so the bank refused it.
entries.contrast: The same verb also means 'go out with someone': They dated for two years.

entries.meaning: To press an official mark onto a document, or to put a postage stamp on a letter. ---
examples: The clerk will stamp your copy.
They stamped my passport at the border.
Send a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

entries.meaning: To put something into an envelope together with a letter. ---
examples: Please enclose a copy of your ID.
She enclosed a check with the form.
A return envelope is enclosed.

entries.meaning: To sign the back of a check, or to say publicly in writing that you support someone. ---
examples: You have to endorse the check before you deposit it.
The paper endorsed her for mayor.
The book is endorsed by two famous novelists.

entries.meaning: To state officially, usually in writing, that something is true or correct. ---
examples: A translator must certify the translation.
The clerk certified the copy for a small fee.
The documents have been certified by a notary.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: certifies, certified, but certifying.

entries.meaning: To have a document officially witnessed and stamped by a notary. ---
examples: The bank can notarize the letter for you.
They notarized the agreement downtown.
The form must be signed and notarized.

entries.meaning: To look at something carefully to make sure it is correct. ---
examples: Check your spelling before you print it.
She checked the figures twice.
He is checking the references at the back.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (check your spelling), intransitive (check before you send it)

entries.meaning: To read students' work and give it a score or a letter. ---
examples: Teachers grade essays on the weekend.
He graded forty papers last night.
The exams are being graded this week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (grade the essays), intransitive (she grades on weekends)
entries.contrast: Americans grade papers; the British mark them.

entries.meaning: To give a test or a piece of work a number of points, or to earn those points. ---
examples: Two readers score each essay.
She scored well on the reading section.
The tests are scored by computer.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (score the tests), intransitive (she scored well)

entries.meaning: To ask someone a set of short questions to test what they know. ---
examples: Quiz me on the new vocabulary.
The teacher quizzed us on chapter four.
She was quizzing her son on the state capitals.
entries.contrast: Doubles the z: quizzes, quizzed, quizzing.

entries.meaning: To do something again and again in order to get better at it. ---
examples: Practice reading out loud.
He practiced his handwriting every evening.
She has been practicing her English on the phone.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (practice your handwriting), intransitive (practice every day)
entries.contrast: American spelling is practice for both noun and verb; British spells the verb practise.

entries.meaning: To write a long article describing a person's life and work. ---
examples: The magazine profiles one scientist a month.
She profiled the mayor last spring.
He is being profiled in Sunday's paper.
entries.русский: писать очерк о ком-либо, делать портрет (в прессе)

entries.meaning: To make a book or a speech shorter by cutting parts of it out. ---
examples: Publishers often abridge long classics for students.
They abridged the novel for the audiobook.
I'd rather read the unabridged version than an abridged one.

entries.meaning: To show clearly in writing that something is important.
examples: These numbers underscore how much reading has changed.
The article underscored the danger of copying without citing.
Her letter is underscoring a point the report ignored.
